facts.claim: World Bank researchers estimate climate change will push 32 million to 132 million additional people into extreme poverty by 2030.
facts.quote: This study shows that the likely short-term impacts of climate change on poverty (32 million to 132 million additional people in extreme poverty by 2030) are of the same orders of magnitude as the impacts of COVID-19 (71 million to 100 million additional people in extreme poverty).

sources.title: Revised Estimates of the Impact of Climate Change on Extreme Poverty by 2030 (Policy Research Working Paper 9417)

facts.notes: Range across thousands of scenarios; optimistic development baselines halve the impact. Health effects (malaria, diarrhea, stunting) and food prices drive most of it; food prices dominate in Sub-Saharan Africa.

facts.claim: The World Bank's Groundswell report finds climate change could force 216 million people across six world regions to move within their countries by 2050, including as many as 86 million in Sub-Saharan Africa.
facts.quote: The World Bank’s updated Groundswell report released today finds that climate change, an increasingly potent driver of migration, could force 216 million people across six world regions to move within their countries by 2050. Hotspots of internal climate migration could emerge as early as 2030 and continue to spread and intensify by 2050. The report also finds that immediate and concerted action to reduce global emissions, and support green, inclusive, and resilient development, could reduce the scale of climate migration by as much as 80 percent. Climate change is a powerful driver of internal migration because of its impacts on people’s livelihoods and loss of livability in highly exposed locations. By 2050, Sub-Saharan Africa could see as many as 86 million internal climate migrants

sources.title: Climate Change Could Force 216 Million People to Migrate Within Their Own Countries by 2050 (Groundswell press release)

facts.notes: Projection under a pessimistic scenario, internal migration only. Other regions: East Asia and the Pacific 49 million, South Asia 40 million, North Africa 19 million, Latin America 17 million, Eastern Europe and Central Asia 5 million.

facts.claim: The latest Lancet Countdown report finds that heat-related mortality per 100,000 has risen 23 per cent since the 1990s, with heat-related deaths averaging 546,000 a year between 2012 and 2021.
facts.quote: It reveals that heat-related mortality per 100,000 has risen 23 per cent since the 1990s, with total heat-related deaths reaching an average of 546,000 annually between 2012 and 2021.

sources.publisher: University College London (host institution of the Lancet Countdown)
sources.title: Climate change inaction costing a life a minute from excessive heat globally (on the 2025 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change)

facts.notes: Global figure, not broken down by income here. The report itself (The Lancet, DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(25)01919-1) returned HTTP 403, so the wording is the Countdown host institution's release. lancetcountdown.org words it "the rate of heat-related deaths surge 23% since the 1990s, to 546,000 a year" (indicator 1.1.5).

facts.claim: Chancel's World Inequality Lab working paper finds that investments represent 70% of emissions from the global top 1% in 2019, up from 58% in 1990.
facts.quote: Most of emissions of top global emitters come from their investments, rather than from their consumption: investments represent 70% of emissions from the global top 1% in 2019, vs. 58% in 1990.

sources.title: Global Carbon Inequality, 1990-2019 (WID.world working paper)

facts.notes: Working-paper version; the peer-reviewed Nature Sustainability abstract says only that "the bulk" of top-1% emissions comes from investments. Another version (28 Feb 2022) says investments are around 50% of global top-10% emissions and slightly above 70% of top-1% emissions in 2019, and under 10% for the bottom 50%. Oxfam (2022) cites this as "50% to 70%".

facts.claim: The latest World Inequality Report finds the poorest half of the global population accounts for only 3% of carbon emissions associated with private capital ownership, while the top 10% account for 77% and the top 1% alone for 41%.
facts.quote: Figure 4 shows that the poorest half of the global population accounts for only 3% of carbon emissions associated with private capital ownership, while the top 10% account for 77% of emissions. The wealthiest 1% alone account for 41% of private capital ownership emissions, almost double the amount of the entire bottom 90% combined.

sources.title: World Inequality Report 2026: Executive Summary

facts.date: December 2025 (World Inequality Report 2026; launch date from press coverage, not printed on the page)
facts.notes: Ownership-based emissions: emissions of privately owned firms and assets allocated to individuals by ownership share; excludes direct household and public-asset emissions (Chancel and Mohren 2025).

facts.claim: The latest World Inequality Report finds that for the top 10%, and especially the top 1%, emissions from capital ownership account for 75–95% of their total footprint in France, Germany and the United States.
facts.quote: For the top 10%, and especially for the top 1%, emissions from capital ownership dominate, accounting for 75–95% of their total footprint in France, Germany, and the United States.

sources.title: World Inequality Report 2026, Chapter 6: Climate, a Capital Problem

facts.date: December 2025 (World Inequality Report 2026; launch date from press coverage, not printed on the page)
facts.notes: Country studies (Chancel and Rehm 2025a). Same chapter: in the US the top 10% account for 24% of consumption-based but 72% of ownership-based emissions; the top 1% from 6% to nearly 43%.

facts.claim: Oxfam finds the investment emissions of 308 billionaires totalled 586 million tonnes of CO2e in 2024, more than the combined emissions of 118 countries.
facts.quote: The investment emissions of the 308 billionaires totalled 586 million tonnes of CO2e in 2024, more than the combined emissions of 118 countries; if they were a country, they would rank as the fifteenth-most polluting country in the world, ahead of South Africa.

sources.title: Climate Plunder: How a powerful few are locking the world into disaster

facts.notes: Scope 1 and 2 emissions of companies in which a billionaire holds at least 10%, allocated in proportion to the stake. Earlier Oxfam estimates used different samples: 125 billionaires, 393 Mt, average 3 Mt (Carbon Billionaires, 2022); 50 billionaires, average ~2.6 Mt (Carbon Inequality Kills, 2024).

facts.claim: Oxfam calculates the average billionaire's annual investment emissions at 1.9 million tonnes of CO2e, 346,000 times more than the average person.
facts.quote: The average billionaire’s annual per capita investment emissions are 1.9 million tonnes of CO2e, which is 346,000 times more than the average person.

sources.title: Climate Plunder: How a powerful few are locking the world into disaster

facts.notes: Sample of 308 billionaires, 2024, Scope 1 and 2 only. DISAGREEMENT across Oxfam editions (different samples): 3 Mt average (2022, 125 billionaires) and ~2.6 Mt (2024, 50 billionaires).

facts.claim: Oxfam finds that counting Scope 3 (value-chain) emissions for 222 billionaires, their total investment emissions in 2024 were 1.85 billion tonnes, equivalent to 4% of global emissions.
facts.quote: Oxfam also identified the Scope 3 emissions – accounting for the whole value chain – of 222 individuals, showing that their total investment emissions in 2024 were 1.85 billion tonnes. This is equivalent to 4% of global emissions and would rank as the fifth-most polluting country in the world.

sources.title: Climate Plunder: How a powerful few are locking the world into disaster

facts.notes: Scope 3 includes emissions from the use of products sold (e.g. burning extracted oil), so it overlaps with other actors' emissions and should not be summed with consumption-based figures.

facts.claim: Oxfam found the average investment emissions of 50 of the world's richest billionaires were around 2.6 million tonnes of CO2e each, around 340 times their emissions from private jets and superyachts combined.
facts.quote: The average investment emissions of 50 of the world's richest billionaires were around 2.6 million tonnes of CO2 equivalents (CO2e) each. That is around 340 times their emissions from private jets and superyachts combined.

sources.title: Carbon Inequality Kills: Why curbing the excessive emissions of an elite few can create a sustainable planet for all

facts.notes: Same report: the private jets of 23 of these billionaires emitted 2,074 tonnes a year on average. Oxfam issued a correction to this report: "In less than a fortnight" (yachts + jets exceed a lifetime of average emissions) should read "In twenty-three days". Do not use the uncorrected line.

facts.claim: Carbon Brief analysis finds the US is responsible for more than a fifth of the 2,651GtCO2 emitted between 1850 and 2025, China for 13% and the 27 EU nations for 12%.
facts.quote: The US is responsible for more than a fifth of the 2,651GtCO2 that humans have pumped into the atmosphere between 1850 and 2025 as a result of fossil fuels, cement and land-use change. China is responsible for another 13% , with the 27 nations of the EU making up another 12%.

sources.title: Analysis: World’s biggest historic polluter – the US – is pulling out of UN climate treaty

facts.notes: Carbon Brief's own analysis (sources: Jones et al. 2023, Lamboll et al. 2023, Global Carbon Project, CDIAC, OWID, IEA, Carbon Monitor). US total 542 GtCO2, China 336, Russia 185. Territorial (production) CO2 incl. land use; country-level, not income-group.

facts.claim: Carbon Brief notes the US population of around 350 million makes up just 4% of the global total, and US per-capita cumulative emissions are around 7 times China's and 25 times India's.
facts.quote: The US share of global warming is even more disproportionate when considering that its population of around 350 million people makes up just 4% of the global total. On the basis of current populations, the US’s per-capita cumulative historical emissions are around 7 times higher than those for China, more than double the EU’s and 25 times those for India.

sources.title: Analysis: World’s biggest historic polluter – the US – is pulling out of UN climate treaty

facts.notes: Same article: US historical emissions (542 GtCO2) exceed the combined total of the 133 lowest-emitting countries, home to more than 3 billion people.

facts.claim: The IPCC finds Least Developed Countries contributed less than 0.4% of historical cumulative fossil-fuel and industry CO2 emissions between 1850 and 2019, while Small Island Developing States contributed 0.5%.
facts.quote: LDCs contributed less than 0.4% of historical cumulative CO2-FFI emissions between 1850 and 2019, while SIDS contributed 0.5%. (high confidence)

sources.title: Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change, Summary for Policymakers (statement B.3.2)

facts.notes: CO2-FFI = fossil fuel and industry CO2 (excludes land use). Same report: total historical net CO2 1850–2019 = 2400 ± 240 GtCO2.

facts.claim: Callahan & Mankin estimate the top five emitters (the United States, China, Russia, Brazil and India) have collectively caused US$6 trillion in income losses from warming since 1990, comparable to 11% of annual global GDP.
facts.quote: We find that the top five emitters (the United States, China, Russia, Brazil, and India) have collectively caused US$6 trillion in income losses from warming since 1990, comparable to 11% of annual global gross domestic product; many other countries are responsible for billions in losses. Yet the distribution of warming impacts from emitters is highly unequal: high-income, high-emitting countries have benefited themselves while harming low-income, low-emitting countries

sources.publisher: Climatic Change (Christopher W. Callahan & Justin S. Mankin)
sources.title: National attribution of historical climate damages

facts.notes: Country-level attribution (territorial emissions) of temperature-driven income changes, 1990 onward; links historical responsibility to measured damages.
